prompt.prompt:
The assignment is:
You will produce the four things a senior engineer should own before a service goes to production: a decision 
record, an autonomy policy, a working evaluation, and an honest measurement plan. Everyone works in the 
same scenario and the same codebase, so the results can be compared and argued about rather than taken on 
trust.
Nothing here has a single right answer. Two people who choose differently from the same question can both do 
well. What separates a strong submission from a weak one is whether the choice is defended against its 
strongest objection, and whether the numbers behind it were measured rather than assumed.
Use whichever approved agent and tools you have.
The scenario
The codebase is ai-in-sdlc-assignment . The scenario around it is in ops/README.md in that repository, along 
with the evidence packs you will need. In short:
You have just been assigned as the senior engineer for the Invoice Approval service. It has run for 18 months as 
an internal tool maintained part-time by one person. In January it becomes a tier-2 service: a 24x7 on-call 
rotation, a published SLO, and a new integration that submits approved invoices to an external payment 
provider, PayEx.
Fact Detail
Team Six engineers, two new to this codebase, one-week on-call rotation
Platform ASP.NET Core 8 on Azure App Service, Azure SQL, GitHub Actions
Available but unused Azure Service Bus is provisioned, and nothing uses it yet
Volume ~40,000 invoices a month, 60% in the last three working days, peaking 
near 80 approvals a minute
Persistence today None. The repository uses an in-memory store, so the database is part of 
going to production
PayEx behavior Returns a reference on success. Times out at 30 seconds, and a timeout 
does not reliably mean the submission failed
Compliance SOC 2 Type II audit in six months. Approval actions auditable for seven 
years
Everything in ops/ describes this planned deployment, not the code as it stands. Keep that distinction: it is the 
subject of the first task.
What to do
An as-built diagram with citations, and one architecture test. Use the Mermaid MCP to produce a 
container view and a sequence diagram for the approval path, citing a file or symbol for every element, 
and list separately everything the agent inferred. Correct whatever is wrong. Then draw the target state 
once persistence and PayEx are in, marking clearly which parts do not exist yet. Finally, encode one 
structural rule as a test that actually runs, with the command written down. One test that runs beats five 
that are described.
2. A decision record on exact-once submission. How do you guarantee an approved invoice reaches PayEx 
exactly once? Consider at least an idempotency key with a dedupe table, a transactional outbox with a 
worker, and optimistic submission with nightly reconciliation. Have the agent lay out the trade-offs, then 
stress it three ways: state a preference for a different option and see whether the recommendation 
moves; ask how your choice fails at 3 a.m. on the last day of the month; ask what it costs to build and to 
run. Write the record yourself, including what would make you revisit it, and a section headed Where the 
agent was wrong or useless, with specifics.
3. An autonomy policy for one workflow. Pick one: month-end log triage, dependency bumps, or firstresponse incident summaries. Write one page covering which tasks sit at which level of autonomy, the 
controls that make that level safe, the evidence needed to move a task up a level, and who approves the 
move. Then state which level this team can run on day one of the rotations, given that two of the six 
engineers are new to the codebase.
4. A review evaluation, run three times. The repository has ten fixed cases in ops/evals. Run the whole set 
three times against one review to prompt and report caught, missed and false alarm rates rather than 
anecdotes. Four of those cases were shown in the session, so add two cases of your own from real defects 
you have seen, at least one of them clean. Then change exactly one thing — the prompt, the model, or the 
context file — and run the set again. Say whether the change was an improvement, and how confident you 
are at that sample size.
5. A risk audit and a measurement plan. Audit the agent setup described at the end of ops/README.md 
against the lethal trifecta: name which legs are present, then either redesign it to remove one or accept 
the risk in writing with the trigger that would make you revisit. Separately, write the baseline you would 
capture before the rotation starts — lead time for changes, change failure rate, review turnaround —
naming the exact source or query for each, and actually capture the two you can get today from the 
repository and its CI history.
The demo video
Record one demo video of 8 to 10 minutes using Teams or using any screen recorder that produces an MP4. 
What to hand in
Mermaid source for the as-built and target diagrams, with the citation list and the inferred-items list
2. One architecture test, with the command that runs it
3. The exactly-once decision record, including the Where the agent was wrong or useless section
4. A one-page autonomy policy, with the day-one level stated
5. Your two added evaluation cases, and a results table covering three runs plus the changed-variable run
6. The risk audit, with a decision recorded
7. The measurement plan, with the two numbers you captured
8. The 8-to-10-minute demo video, uploaded and linked
